title: Pest control principles for food plants, stores and food-service zones
audience: Cleaners and supervisors who work in food plants, stores or food-service zones and who report or respond to pest signs.
learningOutcomes: Explain why pests need controlling before a surface is sanitised.
Describe a pest control programme as an ongoing plan with a named responsible person.
Respond to a pest sign by stopping, recording and reporting, without applying a pesticide unless authorised.
State that pest-control licensing in Australia has not yet been confirmed and that this lesson grants no licence.

instruction.heading: Pests are a sanitation and food-safety problem
instruction.body: Flies, cockroaches, rodents and insects that infest stored food are more than a nuisance. They carry microorganisms on their bodies and can physically contaminate food with fragments, hair, feathers and droppings. Regulators inspect food premises for signs of pests and for conditions that let pests thrive, and contaminated stock can be seized or destroyed. A surface that has been sanitised while pests remain active can be re-contaminated soon afterwards, so sanitising does not hold if the pest question is still open. This is why the order of work matters.

instruction.heading: The order of work and a programme, not a one-off fix
instruction.body: Where nothing is active, the usual order of clean and then sanitise holds. Where pests are active, they are dealt with ahead of the sanitising step. Pest control is a planned programme with named responsibility, scheduled inspections and records. Finding one rodent or one colony of insects is a signal to review the whole area: how incoming stock is inspected, how it is stored, whether the building lets pests in, how housekeeping is done and how often checks are made. Treating only the visible sighting leaves the cause in place and tends to bring the problem back.

instruction.heading: Pesticides, responsibility and the limits of this lesson
instruction.body: Senior management carries the final accountability: it names a capable individual to run the pest programme and backs that person with resources. Anyone who applies a pesticide must use a product that is needed, apply it exactly as the label directs, and confirm that people, food and the environment are not put at risk. Pesticide use is not a task for an untrained cleaner. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to apply a pesticide.

procedure: Stop work in the affected area and keep people away from any droppings, nests or bait.
Do not disturb the sign, and do not move stock that might be needed as evidence until the responsible person decides.
Record the location, the type of sign, the date and the time, with a photo taken with consent where the site allows it.
Report the sign to the responsible person named in the site programme.
Hold new stock out of the affected area until the responsible person clears it.
Do not sanitise the area for food contact until pests are controlled and the responsible person confirms it is safe to proceed.

workedExamples.situation: In a dry store, a worker finds droppings and gnaw marks behind a row of racking, close to stored bagged flour.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first action, and who decides on treatment?
workedExamples.reasoning: The worker stops moving stock into that aisle, records the location and the signs, reports to the responsible person, and does not apply any product. The responsible person decides on inspection and any treatment, and whether the flour is affected.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves and eye protection for any contact with pest debris
Record sheet or device for the sign report
No pesticide is issued for use by a cleaner unless the site has authorised it and the person is trained.

commonErrors.error: Treating a single sighting as a one-off and moving on.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the sign, report it and ask the responsible person to review the whole area.

commonErrors.error: Sanitising a surface while pests are still active.
commonErrors.prevention: Control pests first; sanitise after the responsible person confirms the area is safe.

commonErrors.error: Spraying a product without authority or without reading the label.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not apply pesticides unless authorised, trained and following the label.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring waste and debris as food sources for pests.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat waste areas as a component of the programme (see “Dry waste areas and waste containers as pest and contamination sources”).

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to apply a pesticide.
Pesticide labels set the rate, the method and the protective equipment. Do not apply a product near food, food-contact surfaces or open packaging unless the label and the site plan allow it.
Droppings, nests and dead pests can carry disease. Wear gloves and eye protection, and wash hands after any contact.
The US source states the responsibility principles; Australian application must be checked against the state or territory rules before the lesson is relied on.

qualityStandard: The sign is recorded with location, time and type before anything else is done.
The responsible person is informed in the same shift.
No product is applied by an unauthorised person.
No sanitising of the affected area for food contact occurs until the responsible person clears it.
documentationEvidence: Sign record: location, date, time, type of sign and any photo taken with consent.
Report to the responsible person, with the time it was made.
Stock held or moved and the clearance decision.
summary: Control pests before sanitising; sanitising does not hold while pests are active.
Pest control is a programme with named responsibility, not a one-off task.
Stop, record, report; do not treat without authority.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is pest control completed before sanitising when pests are present?
options: Pests slow sanitisers down for a short time after each visit
Sanitising is not allowed in any building with pests
Pests only attack surfaces that are not sanitised
Pests can re-contaminate a surface that has just been sanitised

knowledgeChecks.question: Which role holds final accountability for the pest programme in a food facility?
options: Top management, which appoints a competent person
The first worker who finds a sign of the pests
The product supplier who sold the bait and the traps
Whoever arrives first each morning and checks the traps

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker finds droppings in a dry store. What is the right first response?
options: Spray the area with the strongest product on hand and close the store for the day
Stop using the area for new stock, record the sign and report it to the responsible person
Sweep the droppings into a bin and close the store later and then keep the stock in place
Move the nearby stock to a different shelf and keep working in the same store
